fig1_spring_work_area.svg: The defining picture of work: $W=\int F\cdot ds$ is the area under the force-displacement curve. For a linear spring $F=kx$ the area is a trapezoid, $\tfrac12k(x_2^2-x_1^2)$ (spring_work), and stretching from 4 to 8 cm takes 1.2 J while the first 4 cm took only 0.4 J — three times cheaper, because the force being worked against is smaller there. The general quadrature work_force_displacement reproduces the same 1.2 J, which is the check that the two agree.
fig2_work_modes.svg: Thermodynamics counts every mode of work in the same currency. A shaft turning at constant torque (shaft_work, $\tau\omega\Delta t$) and a resistor drawing constant current (electric_work, $\mathcal{E}I\Delta t$) both accumulate energy linearly in time, and the slope of each line is that mode's power. Over a minute the 1.8 kW shaft delivers 108 kJ against the 1.2 kW resistor's 72 kJ. Nothing in the energy balance distinguishes their origin — only the sign convention does, work OUT of the system being positive.
